extracted.intended_audience: advertisers, online marketers, telemarketers, and legal/compliance professionals
extracted.subtask_description: A compendium of U.S. Federal Trade Commission enforcement standards and guidance for advertising, telemarketing, infomercials, Internet marketing, spam, privacy, and data security. Covers disclosure, substantiation, prohibited practices, and statutory/regulatory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive format (infomercials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do consumers know that the program they are watching is a commercial?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program-length commercials must not be presented in a way that misleads viewers into thinking they are non-commercial programming. The Commission has challenged deceptive formats in infomercials (e.g., cases alleging failure to disclose commercial nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsubstantiated claims (infomercials and all media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infomercial advertisers must possess the same level of substantiation that would be required to support claims disseminated in any other media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims—including expert endorsements and consumer testimonials—must be supported by competent and reliable evidence. The FTC has repeatedly targeted deceptive or unsubstantiated efficacy and health claims in infomercials and online ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with overlapping consumer protection rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Infomercial and other advertisers must comply with other applicable rules, e.g., Mail Order Rule, Telemarketing Sales Rule, rules on unordered merchandise, unauthorized use of credit cards, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement may be based on multiple statutes/regulations simultaneously; marketers should ensure compliance beyond advertising truthfulness (fulfillment practices, billing, telemarketing rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Telemarketing Sales Rule — required disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Telemarketers must promptly disclose that it is a sales call, the identity of the seller, the nature of the goods or services being offered, and if a prize promotion, that no purchase is necessary to win; certain disclosures must be made before asking for credit card/bank account information or arranging courier pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures must be clear and timely. Failure to make required disclosures has been the basis for numerous enforcement actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telemarketing Sales Rule — bans on misrepresentations
rubrics_metrics.description: The TSR contains broad prohibitions against misrepresentations regarding any required disclosure information and regarding any material aspect of the performance, efficacy, or nature of the goods or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any false or misleading statement about material aspects of the offer or the terms may violate Section 5 and the TSR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telemarketing Sales Rule — authorization for debits and billing
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits telemarketers from debiting checking accounts without the consumer's express, verifiable authorization and from making misleading statements to induce consumers to pay for goods or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verifiable authorization standards must be followed; unauthorized debits and misleading inducements have led to civil penalties and injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telemarketing Sales Rule — assisting and facilitating liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Bars anyone from giving substantial assistance to a telemarketer when the person knows or consciously avoids knowing that the telemarketer is engaged in conduct that would violate certain provisions of the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third parties (processors, lead generators, platform providers) can be liable if they knowingly facilitate TSR violations; enforcement includes suits against facilitators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telemarketing Sales Rule — calling time and do-not-call restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits calling consumers before 8 a.m. and after 9 p.m., and from calling consumers who have said they do not want to be called.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telemarketers must implement time-of-day restrictions and honor consumer opt-outs; violations are actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telemarketing Sales Rule — civil penalties & dual enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of the rule may result in civil penalties of up to $11,000; the rule is enforceable by the FTC and by state attorneys general, who can obtain nationwide orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential for high monetary sanctions and statewide/nationwide injunctions; compliance programs should account for multi-jurisdictional enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do-Not-Call Registry — enrollment and list scrubbing
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers may enroll in a national do-not-call registry; telemarketers are required to scrub their lists regularly of consumers who do not wish to receive such calls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain current suppression lists and document scrubbing processes; failure to scrub lists has been the basis of penalties and settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do-Not-Call Rule — call-abandonment, caller ID, and charitable solicitation disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rule imposes new restrictions on call abandonment, requires telemarketers to transmit Caller ID, and (pursuant to the USA PATRIOT Act) requires telemarketers soliciting charitable contributions to promptly disclose the organization and that the purpose is to ask for a contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special rules apply to charity calls; ensure systems do not engage in call-abandonment practices and that Caller ID is transmitted correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do-Not-Call Rule — ban on unauthorized billing and express informed consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Bans unauthorized billing and prohibits telemarketers from processing any billing information for payment without the express informed consent of the customer or donor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain and document clear, informed consent before processing payments; unauthorized billing violations have resulted in multimillion-dollar penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone Disclosure and Dispute Resolution Act — 900-number disclosures and child protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trade Regulation Rule pursuant to the Act addresses advertising, operating standards, and billing for 900 numbers; requires specific disclosures such as the cost of the call and that individuals under 18 must have parental permission to call; prohibits advertising directed to children under 12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers of pay-per-call services must disclose call costs clearly and follow age-targeting restrictions; violations have led to enforcement actions with substantial relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet advertising — substantiation and Dot Com Disclosures guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission applies the same well-established principles of substantiation to Internet advertising as it applies in any other media; see staff working paper 'Dot Com Disclosures' for guidance on applying rules online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online claims require the same competent and reliable evidence as offline claims. Disclosures placed online (e.g., in metatags, mouseover text) must be clear and conspicuous where consumers will see them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive online techniques prohibited (pagejacking, mouse trapping, metatag misuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices such as duplicating legitimate websites to divert users (pagejacking), disabling back/exit commands (mouse trapping), deceptive use of metatags/mouseover text/hyperlinks, and other techniques that mislead or trap users are actionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and technical behavior of online pages must not mislead or coerce consumers; several FTC cases have targeted these specific practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mail Order Rule and timely shipping/fulfillment online
rubrics_metrics.description: Online sellers must comply with the Mail Order Rule (e.g., shipping within promised timeframes) and disclose delays; failure to ship as represented can be deceptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project TooLate.com and related enforcement actions show the FTC will pursue shipping/fulfillment misrepresentations during high-volume periods (e.g., holidays).

rubrics_metrics.name: CAN-SPAM / unsolicited commercial email requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Final regulations under CAN-SPAM establish standards to determine whether an e-mail message has a commercial primary purpose and is subject to the Act; requirements include accurate header information, truthful subject lines, a functioning opt-out mechanism, a valid physical postal address, and identification when sexually explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial emails must include clear opt-out methods honored promptly, not disguise origin or subject, and include a valid postal address. FTC cases enforced failures such as missing opt-outs, invalid addresses, misleading headers/subjects, and failure to honor unsubscribe requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on header/subject line spoofing and disguise
rubrics_metrics.description: Disguising commercial emails as personal messages or forging header information (spoofing) is deceptive and actionable under Section 5 and CAN-SPAM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure mail systems set accurate header fields and that subject lines reflect message content; enforcement includes significant civil penalties for disguised/spoofed messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illicit use of consumer computers (spam zombies / hijacking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tapping into consumers' home computers to send spam (botnets/spam zombies) or hijacking computers to deliver deceptive messages is illegal and targeted by coordinated enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical and operational security to prevent compromise is required; operations that commandeer consumer machines have been the subject of coordinated international actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy — Fair Information Practices (core principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC identified four core principles of fair information practices for online privacy: Notice, Choice, Access, and Security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Websites should provide notice of data collection and uses, give consumers meaningful choice, permit access to review/modify/delete data, and implement appropriate security measures. FTC Reports to Congress recommend these as baseline standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy — reasonable data security and truthful security claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies must take reasonable security measures to protect sensitive customer data and must not make false claims about implementing security measures (e.g., claiming encryption when not used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to secure consumer data or misrepresentations about security practices have been challenged as unfair practices; enforcement includes consent orders, disgorgement, and penalties tied to breaches and false promises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy — honoring privacy policies and prohibiting unauthorized disclosure/sale
rubrics_metrics.description: Promises in published privacy policies (e.g., that information will not be disclosed to third parties) are enforceable; selling or disclosing personal information contrary to those promises violates Section 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure privacy policies accurately reflect data-sharing practices and obtain necessary consents before sharing/selling data collected under a particular representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spyware/adware — disclosure, consent, and uninstallability
rubrics_metrics.description: Downloading adware/spyware onto consumers' computers without clear and conspicuous disclosure, and obstructing its removal, is an unfair and deceptive practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software bundling must be disclosed in a clear and conspicuous manner; consumers must be able to remove unwanted software. Cases have resulted in disgorgement and injunctions against companies that installed or hid spyware/adware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral advertising and online profiling — transparency and regulatory scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracking consumers online to target advertising (behavioral advertising) and online profiling raise consumer protection and privacy issues; the FTC has convened workshops and issued reports urging transparency and self-regulation complemented by potential legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies engaging in tracking/profiling should adopt clear notices, meaningful choice mechanisms, and consider industry self-regulatory standards (e.g., NAI), while noting potential future legislative requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data breach and third-party data security liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies that fail to take appropriate security measures for sensitive consumer information or that permit unauthorized disclosures can be charged with unfair trade practices and face civil penalties and redress obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement and document reasonable security controls, vendor management, and breach response procedures; enforcement actions (including multi-million-dollar settlements) have followed large breaches and lax security practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising targeting children and collection from minors
rubrics_metrics.description: Special protections apply when collecting personal information from children and targeting advertising to minors (e.g., prohibitions on advertising to children under 12 in pay-per-call context; extra scrutiny for data collection from children as young as ten).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply with child-directed advertising rules and COPPA-related expectations; disclosures and limits on collection/use/transfer of children's data are critical to avoid enforcement.
